title: Same-Day TAVR and Femur Fracture Repair in a 103-Year-Old Woman: Beyond Chronologic Age.
authors: Rahul Gupta; Matthew P Sullivan; Syed T Ali; Reza Gorji; Callistus Ditah; Ankur Kalra
abstract:
A 103-year-old woman with critical nonrheumatic calcific aortic stenosis was transferred to an academic medical center after an urgent femoral fracture fixation was deferred because of high perioperative cardiac risk.
Why was transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) chosen before orthopedic surgery, and why was balloon aortic valvuloplasty not an optimal bridge? What was the severity and clinical impact of post-TAVR aortic regurgitation? How did procedural risk influence sedation and anesthesia? How did multidisciplinary teams coordinate expedited care?
TAVR was performed to reduce intraoperative cardiac risk, followed by open reduction and internal fixation later the same day. Structural heart, anesthesia, orthopedic, rehabilitation, and social work teams coordinated expedited treatment and recovery planning.
Severe aortic stenosis and acute fracture require coordinated, time-sensitive management. TAVR may facilitate timely orthopedic surgery and reduce immobilization-related decline. Candidacy should consider frailty, functional status, physiologic reserve, procedural risk, recovery potential, and patient goals, not age alone.

title: The Ross procedure: Technical principles, operative strategy, and pitfalls for long-term success.
authors: Bahaaldin Alsoufi
abstract: The Ross procedure remains an attractive aortic valve replacement strategy for children, adolescents, and selected young adults. Pulmonary autograft replacement provides excellent hemodynamics, freedom from anticoagulation, growth potential in children, and favorable long-term survival in appropriately selected patients. These advantages, however, come at the cost of substantial technical complexity. Small imperfections during autograft harvest, implantation, coronary transfer, or root reconstruction can result in early dysfunction, coronary complications, or late autograft dilatation and failure. The purpose of this review is to summarize a practical and reproducible approach to the Ross procedure with emphasis on operative strategy, technical details, Ross-Konno modifications, autograft stabilization techniques, and avoidance of common pitfalls. Rather than advocating a single technique, we emphasize fundamental principles that permit adaptation to patient anatomy while maintaining the geometric integrity of the left ventricular outflow tract, aortic root, and pulmonary root.

title: Myocardial Infarction in a Patient With Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia: Acalabrutinib-Related Dehoming as a Potential Culprit.
authors: Louis Therrien; Dany Burke
abstract: Patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) frequently suffer from atherosclerosis and its conventional risk factors. Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitor therapy is known to impact coronary and vascular risk. We report the case of a 71-year-old woman with CLL treated with a second-generation BTK inhibitor, well-controlled hypertension, and asymptomatic carotid stenosis who presented with an anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) complicated by complete heart block shortly after beginning treatment with acalabrutinib. The patient was found to have significant treatment-related redistribution lymphocytosis following the initiation of BTK inhibitor therapy, with an absolute lymphocyte count (ALC) of 261 x 109/L on admission. Despite a complicated clinical course including cardiac arrest, third-degree atrioventricular heart block requiring temporary transvenous pacing, cardiac ischemia treated with percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) and intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP), and parietal and occipital strokes, she was ultimately discharged to a rehabilitation facility and subsequently returned home. We describe a patient with previously unrecognized severe multivessel coronary artery disease who developed a STEMI 28 days after acalabrutinib initiation in the setting of marked treatment-associated lymphocytosis. We hypothesize that redistribution lymphocytosis may have contributed to coronary plaque destabilization and subsequent myocardial infarction in the presence of pre-existing atherosclerotic disease, although causality cannot be established. This observation is hypothesis-generating and highlights the need for cardiovascular vigilance during the early weeks of BTK inhibitor therapy.

title: Secondary aldosteronism due to premature renal artery atherosclerosis in X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy.
authors: Nicole van Rossum; Pascale Boily; Marco Lefebvre; André C Carpentier; Matthieu St-Jean
abstract: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (ALD), an uncommon cause of adrenal insufficiency, requires lifelong surveillance of adrenal function. Glucocorticoid deficiency is reported in approximately 80% and mineralocorticoid deficiency in 50% of patients with ALD. In 2014, we took over the follow-up of a 31-year-old man who had been diagnosed with ALD in 1991. In 1995, he was treated with hematopoietic stem cell transplantation and was supplemented with hydrocortisone 10 mg/m2 and fludrocortisone 0.05 mg daily. In 2015, resistant hypertension and hypokalemia were noticed and persisted despite discontinuation of fludrocortisone. Biochemical analysis showed secondary aldosteronism. Doppler ultrasonography was compatible with a hemodynamically significant right renal artery stenosis. Furthermore, significant aortic atheromatosis was described on abdominal computed tomography, which was disproportionate for the patient's age and risk factors. Spironolactone was added to his antihypertensive medication, which normalized blood pressure and hypokalemia. In 2022, he presented with severe hypotension and acute renal failure. All his antihypertensive medications were stopped because secondary aldosteronism had been resolved. The renal Doppler showed severe right renal artery stenosis with severe renal atrophy. Thus, he spontaneously infarcted his right kidney that was inducing secondary aldosteronism, confirming he had persistent inducible zona glomerulosa cells.

title: Platelet-endothelial crosstalk drives distinct endothelial dysfunction in bicuspid aortic valve disease.
authors: Luisa Weiss; Sarvesh Chelvanambi; Amarri Harrison; Taku Kasai; Yuto Nakamura; Mandy E Turner; Mark C Blaser; Marie Billaud; Masanori Aikawa; Sasha A Singh; Elena Aikawa
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract:
Bicuspid aortic valves (BAV) predispose individuals to premature development of aortic stenosis (AS). The abnormal hemodynamic environment of BAV affects both platelets and valvular endothelial cells (VECs), but whether platelet-derived signals contribute to valve morphology-specific endothelial dysfunction remains unknown.
Platelets and VECs were obtained from patients with BAVs or tricuspid aortic valves (TAVs) undergoing valve replacement for AS. Platelets were activated to generate platelet releasate (PR). PR composition and its effects on VECs were investigated using complementary molecular, multi-omic, functional, and computational approaches.
BAV and TAV patients exhibited markedly distinct PR profiles, which translated into differential endothelial responses. Strikingly, BAV-derived PR elicited a substantially more pronounced endothelial dysfunction phenotype, characterized by widespread molecular reprogramming and functional alterations. Integrated multi-omics uncovered mitochondrial dysfunction as a central feature of BAV PR-induced endothelial injury, accompanied by activation of pathways spanning endothelial remodeling, migration, and immune-cell recruitment. These molecular signatures translated into mitochondrial depolarization, altered mitochondrial dynamics, enhanced VEC migration, and increased neutrophil adhesion and chemotaxis. Finally, computational ligand-receptor and ligand-target analyses identified candidate signaling axes linking platelet-derived mediators to endothelial reprogramming, highlighting potential therapeutic targets.
We provide the first direct evidence that platelet activation contributes to AS initiation through the induction of endothelial dysfunction and that these effects are amplified in BAV. These findings identify platelet-VEC crosstalk as a previously unrecognized mechanism linking abnormal valve hemodynamics to disease onset. Targeting platelet-derived mediators may represent a novel therapeutic strategy for AS, specifically in BAV.
Bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) confers a substantial risk of premature aortic stenosis, yet no pharmacological therapy to halt disease development exists. Our findings position platelet-endothelial crosstalk as a mechanistic link between the abnormal hemodynamic environment of BAV and valvular endothelial dysfunction. Platelet-derived mediators promoted endothelial remodeling, mitochondrial dysfunction, and a migratory phenotype, with more marked effects in BAV. These observations suggest that platelets actively contribute to the initiation and progression of calcific aortic valve disease rather than solely reflecting advanced stenosis. Targeting shear-dependent platelet-endothelial signaling may therefore provide new opportunities for sought-after disease-modifying therapeutic strategies in (BAV-associated) aortic stenosis.

title: Multiparametric Extracellular Vesicle Profiling Identifies a Distinct Circulating Signature of Bicuspid Aortic Valve Disease.
authors: Luisa Weiss; Amarri Harrison; Sarvesh Chelvanambi; Taku Kasai; Mandy E Turner; Mark C Blaser; Marie Billaud; Masanori Aikawa; Sasha A Singh; Elena Aikawa
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract:
Calcific aortic valve disease (CAVD) resulting in life-threatening aortic stenosis, heart failure and death, develops earlier and progresses more rapidly in patients with bicuspid aortic valves (BAV) than tricuspid aortic valves (TAV), yet the circulating molecular drivers remain poorly understood. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) capture disease-relevant cellular activation and offer a powerful window into a BAV-specific pathophysiology.
Circulating large extracellular vesicle (LEV) abundance and morphology were characterized by complementary single-vesicle nano-flow cytometry and super-resolution microscopy. Proteomic profiling further delineated LEV molecular cargoes and associated biological pathways between patients with BAV and TAV.
We demonstrate that patients with BAVs exhibited fundamentally altered circulating LEV profiles compared to TAVs. Super-resolution imaging revealed BAV-specific organization of platelet- and leukocyte-associated adhesion molecules into discrete EV membrane microdomains. Proteomic profiling identified distinct LEV cargoes between BAV and TAV, including a BAV-specific, previously unrecognized neutrophil-associated signature enriched for proteins involved in neutrophil degranulation and innate immunity. Consistent with this phenotype, BAV displayed alterations in platelet- and neutrophil-associated LEV populations, suggesting enhanced (thrombo-)inflammatory activity. Lastly, distinct associations between LEV populations and clinical parameters in BAV and TAV suggest that LEV profiles reflect morphology-specific aspects of disease severity.
Comprehensive single-vesicle analysis and bulk proteomic profiling identified a distinct circulating LEV signature in BAV-associated CAVD, characterized by endothelial activation and reciprocal platelet-neutrophil interactions. These findings reveal previously unrecognized differences in circulating LEVs between BAV and TAV and highlight their potential as biomarkers of valve morphology-specific pathophysiology.

title: Long-term outcomes following balloon aortic valvuloplasty for congenital aortic stenosis in children: a 29-year single-centre experience.
authors: Zeynep Gulben Kuk Ozalp; Gerald Riordan; Elizabeth Alok; Elie Sawan; Javid Raja; Jacqueline Nguyen Khuong; Philip Roberts; Ian Nicholson
abstract:
Initial treatment of critical aortic stenosis in children, balloon or surgical aortic valvuloplasty, remains debated. Our centre used the balloon procedure first in almost all patients for over 29 years, a predominantly balloon-first cohort.
To characterise long-term outcomes of balloon aortic valvuloplasty as first-line treatment for critical aortic stenosis.
We retrospectively reviewed 201 patients treated between June 1996 and December 2025, grouped as neonates (0-28 days), infants (29-365 days), and children (>365 days). Freedom from surgery and reintervention were analysed with the Kaplan-Meier method; categorical comparisons used chi-square tests.
Median follow-up was 9 years. Aortic valve surgery was required in 78 patients (38.8%), most commonly a Ross or Ross-Konno procedure (49, 62.8%). Neonates required surgery more often than infants and children (36/74, 48.6% versus 42/127, 33.1%; p = 0.042); median time to surgery in neonates was 6 months. One-year Kaplan-Meier freedom from surgery was 63% in neonates, 91% in infants, and 96% in children. Moderate-to-severe post-procedural valve dysfunction was associated with more surgery than mild dysfunction (49.3% versus 33.3%; p = 0.041). Kaplan-Meier freedom from any reintervention was 47% at 10 years and 31% at 15 years. Mortality was 3.5% overall and 8.1% in neonates, mostly in the early era.
Balloon aortic valvuloplasty is an effective first-line treatment for infants and children with critical aortic stenosis. However, many neonates need surgery within the first year, usually a Ross procedure. In centres with experienced cardiac surgeons, surgical aortic valvuloplasty could be considered a reasonable alternative initial approach for neonates.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Cardiac Auscultation for Detecting Clinically Significant Valvular Heart Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
authors: Humza Saeed; Tameem Bin Nasir; Ayesha Rehman; Uzair Majeed; Ishtiaq Hussain; Salman Khalid; Naeem Khan Tahirkheli
abstract: Early identification of clinically significant valvular heart disease (VHD) remains challenging because echocardiography is resource-intensive and conventional auscultation is operator-dependent. Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled analysis of digital heart sounds has emerged as a promising screening strategy, but its overall diagnostic performance has not been systematically evaluated. We conducted a Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses of Diagnostic Test Accuracy studies-compliant systematic review and diagnostic test accuracy meta-analysis of studies evaluating AI-enabled cardiac auscultation against transthoracic echocardiography for detecting clinically significant VHD, defined according to each study's echocardiographic criteria. MEDLINE, Embase, and CENTRAL were searched through July 2026, and pooled sensitivity, specificity, summary receiver operating characteristic area under the curve, diagnostic odds ratio, and accuracy were estimated using random-effects models. Eight studies comprising 4374 analyzed participants were included. AI-enabled cardiac auscultation demonstrated a pooled sensitivity of 72% (95% CI 54-85%) and specificity of 82% (95% CI 74-88%) for detecting clinically significant VHD. The summary receiver operating characteristic area under the curve was 0.814 (95% CI 0.569-0.888), and the pooled diagnostic odds ratio was 11.39 (95% CI 3.76-34.47), corresponding to positive and negative likelihood ratios of approximately 4.0 and 0.34, respectively. Overall pooled diagnostic accuracy was 78% (95% CI 67-86%). Subgroup analyses demonstrated substantially higher sensitivity for studies evaluating isolated aortic stenosis than composite VHD (92% vs. 55%; P < 0.001), whereas specificity was comparable. AI-enabled cardiac auscultation demonstrates promising diagnostic performance for identifying clinically significant VHD and may serve as a front-line screening tool to prioritize patients for echocardiography. Future prospective multicenter studies using standardized recording protocols and external validation are needed before widespread clinical implementation.

title: Multistage cardiac surgery, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, and advanced wound care in a critically ill neonate: a case report.
authors: Gianluca Castiello; Alessandro Giamberti; Alessandro Varrica; Matteo Reali; Mauro Lo Rito; Federica Torchio; Giuseppe Isgrò; Angela Satriano; Corinne Messina; Massimo Chessa; Greta Ghizzardi; Rosario Caruso
abstract:
Neonates with complex congenital heart disease (CHD) frequently require early and staged surgical interventions, which carry a high risk of postoperative complications. The coexistence of an interrupted aortic arch, ventricular septal defect (VSD), and mitral valve stenosis represents a rare and particularly high-risk constellation. This case is noteworthy for the integration of multistage cardiac surgery, prolonged extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), and an innovative wound management strategy combining negative pressure wound therapy (NPWT) with topical oxygen-enriched gel.
We report the case of a one-month-old Romanian female infant diagnosed with type A interrupted aortic arch, VSD, and mitral valve stenosis. The initial surgical procedure included aortic arch reconstruction, VSD closure with a bovine pericardial patch, and mitral valve repair. Severe residual mitral regurgitation necessitated immediate initiation of veno-arterial ECMO, followed by mitral valve replacement with a Melody bioprosthesis. On postoperative day 19, thrombotic obstruction of the prosthetic valve required a third surgical intervention for clot removal, after which ECMO was discontinued. Delayed sternal closure was performed on day 26, but wound dehiscence developed on day 33. Management included NPWT combined with topical oxygen-enriched gel for 33 days, followed by gel monotherapy for 38 additional days. Complete secondary intention healing was achieved after 73 days. Despite developing Pseudomonas aeruginosa sepsis and late-onset Staphylococcus haemolyticus bacteremia, the patient recovered fully without neurological deficits or wound-related sequelae.
This case highlights the feasibility of combining advanced surgical management with innovative wound care strategies in critically ill neonates with complex CHD. The successful integration of NPWT and topical oxygen therapy promoted wound healing after delayed sternal closure, even in the context of severe infection and prolonged ECMO support. These findings suggest that tailored, multidisciplinary approaches may optimize outcomes in high-complexity neonatal cardiac cases.

title: Superficial temporal artery pressure monitoring as an adjunct to regional cerebral oxygen saturation during transcarotid transcatheter aortic valve replacement: a case report.
authors: Naoki Awaya; Satoshi Jujo; Hidehiko Okuma; Yuji Kato; Kenichi Ueda
abstract:
Transcarotid transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TC-TAVR) requires common carotid artery (CCA) clamping, necessitating cerebral perfusion monitoring. Regional cerebral oxygen saturation (rSO2) is widely used but limited by extracranial contamination. Superficial temporal artery (STA) pressure monitoring may reflect collateral perfusion pressure distal to the clamp because of ipsilateral internal carotid artery (ICA)-STA continuity during CCA clamping.
An 80-year-old man with severe aortic stenosis underwent TC-TAVR via the left CCA. Under ultrasound guidance, we placed a 24-gauge catheter in the left STA to monitor collateral perfusion pressure during CCA clamping. STA mean arterial pressure (MAP) decreased from 81 to 35 mmHg upon CCA clamping and was targeted at ≥ 40 mmHg with norepinephrine, except during rapid pacing for valve deployment. He was discharged on postoperative day 5 uneventfully.
STA pressure may provide supplementary collateral perfusion information to rSO2 during CCA clamping, and ultrasound-guided STA cannulation was feasible.

title: Prognostic utility of transvalvular flow rate in patients with low-gradient aortic stenosis undergoing transcatheter aortic valve implantation.
authors: Binyang Xi; Kyohei Usami; Kimi Sato; Naoto Kawamatsu; Masayoshi Yamamoto; Tomoko Machino-Ohtsuka; Daigo Hiraya; Hiroaki Watabe; Tomoya Hoshi; Tomoko Ishizu; Yoshihiro Seo; JSE-TAVI Investigators
abstract:
Flow assessment helps determine the severity of low-gradient (LG) aortic stenosis (AS). Transvalvular flow rate (FR) may classify flow status differently from stroke volume index (SVi). This study compared their prognostic utility in patients with LG-AS undergoing transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI).
This post hoc analysis of a multicenter registry included 205 patients with severe symptomatic LG-AS who underwent TAVI. Low flow (LF) was defined separately as SVi ≤35 mL/m2 or FR ≤200 mL/s. The primary endpoint was all-cause death.
SVi classified 74 patients (36%) as having LF, whereas FR classified 131 (64%) as having LF, including 63 with normal flow according to SVi. FR was correlated with LVEF (r = 0.457, P < 0.001) and natural-log-transformed E/e' (r = -0.205, P = 0.010). Patients with LF according to either measure showed greater recovery in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF). In the multivariable Cox model, FR ≤200 mL/s was not associated with all-cause mortality (HR, 0.764; 95% CI, 0.376-1.551; P = 0.456).
FR identified more patients with LF than SVi but did not show an association with outcome after TAVI. These findings do not support prioritizing FR over SVi in patients with LG-AS.

title: Cardiogenic shock phenotypes and outcomes under percutaneous left ventricular support: results from a 9-year single-center real-world cohort.
authors: Georgios Chatzis; Styliani Syntila; Harald Schuett; Harald Lapp; Carlo-Federico Fichera; Bernhard Schieffer; Bjoern Goebel; Birgit Markus; Julian Kreutz; Kiarash Sassani; Christian Waechter; Felix Ausbuettel; Fares Kano
journal: Clinical research in cardiology : official journal of the German Cardiac Society
abstract:
Refractory cardiogenic shock (CS) remains associated with unacceptably high mortality despite advances in intensive-care and coronary intervention strategies. Percutaneous left ventricular support using Impella is widely used, yet real-world outcomes may differ substantially by underlying shock etiology and phenotype.
We performed a retrospective single-center cohort study of adults treated with Impella 2.5/CP for refractory CS over a 9-year period. Patients were classified as acute coronary syndrome (ACS), dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM)/myocarditis, severe aortic stenosis (AS), sepsis-associated CS, or other causes. Endpoints were all-cause in-hospital and 12-month mortality. Multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, lactate, vasoactive score, Impella type was conducted; a sensitivity model additionally included creatinine.
Among 409 patients (mean age 69.99 ± 11.56 years; 75.6% male), ACS was the leading phenotype (n = 269), followed by DCM/myocarditis (n = 53), AS (n = 32), sepsis-associated CS (n = 36), and other causes (n = 19). Impella CP was used in 227 patients (55.5%). Overall in-hospital mortality was 48.9% and differed across phenotypes, being highest in sepsis-associated CS (80.6%; chi-squared p < 0.001). Sepsis remained independently associated with in-hospital death after adjustment (adjusted odds ratio 4.65, 95% CI 2.03-12.07, p = 0.0006) for major confounders; finding was consistent after additional adjustment for creatinine (adjusted odds ratio 4.17, 95% CI 1.63-12.26, p = 0.0023). Major bleeding occurred in 14.9%, limb ischemia in 11.7%, pseudoaneurysm in 4.9%, and stroke in 1.0% of the patients. Twelve-month survival analysis also demonstrated phenotype-dependent patterns (log-rank p < 0.01).
In refractory CS treated with Impella outcomes are strongly phenotype-dependent. Sepsis-associated CS represents an extreme-risk phenotype with poor short- and long-term survival, suggesting phenotype-guided patient selection and prospective validation of escalation strategies.

title: Robotic aortic valve replacement with a sutureless valve, through a 3 cm transaxillary incision: a step-by-step surgical guide.
authors: Saurabh Varshney; Shreya Varshney; Manish Sonkusale
journal: Multimedia manual of cardiothoracic surgery : MMCTS
abstract: Robotic aortic valve replacement remains a challenging procedure, limiting its widespread adoption. We present our technique of robotic aortic valve replacement with da Vinci X system, with a sutureless valve (Perceval Plus), where we have tried to simplify the procedural steps. These can be very easily adopted by surgeons worldwide. The procedure includes port placement, docking, incision planning, femoral cannulation, aortotomy, valve excision, implantation tips for the sutureless valve, and aortotomy closure. The refinement of this approach has been associated with rapid postoperative recovery, with the patient walking in less than 24 hours after surgery. This step-by-step video tutorial will help surgeons worldwide in the adoption of robotic aortic valve replacement techniques.

title: Bicuspidization of a severely dysplastic aortic valve in a neonate.
authors: Ivan Kozyrev; Mathieu Vergnat; Philipp Suchowerskyj; Benjamin Bierbach; Claudia Arenz; Boulos Asfour
journal: Multimedia manual of cardiothoracic surgery : MMCTS
abstract: Severe congenital aortic valve stenosis in neonates remains a challenging lesion requiring individualized treatment. While balloon aortic valvuloplasty and surgical valvotomy are established treatment options, neonates with severely dysplastic valve morphology may benefit from anatomical valve reconstruction in addition to relief of obstruction. This video tutorial demonstrates our technique of bicuspidization of a severely dysplastic neonatal aortic valve by commissural reconstruction, extensive leaflet shaving and limited free-edge remodelling. Our ultimate goal of tricuspid valve repair was impossible in this scenario.

title: Transaxillary direct-view aortic valve replacement with Intuity Elite rapid-deployment valve.
authors: Michele Galeazzi; Erlil Mali; Simone D'Alessio; Martina Giusti; Carlo Zingaro; Pietro Malvindi; Paolo Berretta; Marco Di Eusanio
journal: Multimedia manual of cardiothoracic surgery : MMCTS
abstract: We present a minimally invasive aortic valve replacement performed through a right transaxillary minithoracotomy. This approach uses a single 4-5 cm lateral incision, minimizing chest wall trauma while providing excellent cosmetic results. It redefines surgical perspective by offering a direct, non-mediated view of the aortic valve with a naturally perpendicular trajectory to the annular plane. This results in optimal eye-hand alignment, shorter working distance and enhanced operative control, simplifying the procedure, not only compared to endoscopic or robotic techniques, but also to right anterior minithoracotomy, where direct vision is obtained through a less favourable trajectory and a more limited anterior intercostal space. The procedure is performed using standard instruments and standardized set-up, without the need for specialized or expensive technologies, improving reproducibility and scalability. Its intrinsic simplicity makes it particularly suited for fast-track protocols, facilitating on-table extubation and early mobilization. The combination with rapid-deployment valves further streamlines the operation by reducing cardiopulmonary bypass and cross-clamp times, while the transaxillary exposure ensures accurate annular alignment and controlled, symmetrical deployment. In this case, the patient was extubated on-table and discharged home after 5 days, illustrating how this approach can simplify minimally invasive aortic valve surgery while maintaining safety and precision.

title: Aortic Root Remodeling Patterns and Outcomes Five Years Following Contemporary Root Replacement Strategies in Young Patients: A Single-Center Experience.
authors: Obieze Nwanna-Nzewunwa; Mayowa Otoruko; Robert D B Jaquiss; Nicholas D Andersen; Ryan R Davies; Karl M Reyes
journal: World journal for pediatric & congenital heart surgery
abstract: Background: Long-term dimensional remodeling patterns after contemporary aortic root operations in young patients have historically not been well characterized and this may inform surgical decision-making.Methods: We evaluated longitudinal aortic root and annular remodeling patterns and clinical outcomes after the Bentall, Ross, or Valve-Sparing Root procedures from January 1, 2000 to December 31, 2024.Results: Sixty patients underwent aortic root replacement. Of these, 17 had the Bentall procedure (BP), 20 had the Ross procedure, and 23 had Valve Sparing Aortic Root Replacement (VSARR). On average Ross patients (4 years) were younger than BP (16 years) and VSARR (16 years) (p = .0001). Marfans (20%, 12/60), Down Syndrome (3%, 2/60) and Loeys-Dietz (3%, 2/60) were prevalent. All Marfan patients (n = 12) underwent VSARR (p = .006). The leading surgical indications were aortic regurgitation (78%, 47/60), aortic stenosis (58%, 35/60), and aortic aneurysm (46%, 28/60). Mortality rate was 7% (n = 4/60) and no statistically significant difference in survival was observed (p = .94). Reoperation occurred in 3 of 60 patients (5%). Four of 60 patients (7%) had endocarditis. At 5 years, the change in aortic root size was significantly different across operation types (p = .041), with significant dilation noted in the Ross cohort.Conclusions: Ross patients demonstrated greater neoaortic root enlargement at 5 years, although valve competence was generally preserved. Given the differences in age, underlying pathology, and surgical selection among the groups, these findings should be interpreted as descriptive remodeling patterns rather than evidence of the superiority of one operative strategy.

title: Pooled Periprocedural and Short-Term Outcomes After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement With Contemporary Self-Expanding Valves: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
authors: Shawn Shaji; Praveen Bharath Saravanan; Rahul Sarkar; Chloe Kharsa; Joe Aoun; Syed Zaid; Waleed T Kayani; Nadeen Faza; Stephen H Little; Marvin Atkins; Fernando Ramirez Del Val; Neal S Kleiman; Michael J Reardon; Sahar Samimi; Sachin S Goel
journal: Structural heart : the journal of the Heart Team
abstract:
Contemporary self-expanding transcatheter heart valves (SEVs) have incorporated design refinements to reduce paravalvular leak (PVL) and pacemaker implantation (PPI). We aimed to characterize clinical outcomes after transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) with contemporary SEVs in patients with severe aortic stenosis.
PubMed, EMBASE, and Scopus were searched through October 5, 2025, for studies reporting procedural, hemodynamic, and clinical outcomes for patients undergoing TAVR with the (1) Navitor or (2) Evolut PRO/PRO+/FX. Random-effects meta-analyses pooled single-arm event rates, stratified by SEV group, using the Freeman-Tukey double arcsine transformation. Between-platform differences were assessed using subgroup interaction testing.
Fifty-two studies (n = 21,349; weighted mean age 82 years; mean Society of Thoracic Surgeons Predicted Risk of Mortality 4.8%) were included. At 30 days, all-cause mortality was low among Evolut and Navitor cohorts (1.4 and 1.5%; p = 0.63), and device success was high for both platforms (92.1 and 93.0%; p = 0.73). Moderate or greater PVL occurred in 2.5 and 1.1% of Evolut and Navitor cohorts, respectively (p = 0.12), mild PVL occurred in 31.1 and 19.9% (p = 0.046), and new PPI occurred in 13.4 and 15.3%, respectively. Mean gradients remained low among Evolut and Navitor cohorts at 1 year (7.7 and 7.3 mmHg; p = 0.65), whereas effective orifice area was higher among Evolut cohorts at 1 year (2.1 and 1.8 cm2; p < 0.001) (p = p-interaction).
Navitor and Evolut PRO/PRO+/FX both demonstrated high device success, low mortality, favorable hemodynamic performance, and low rates of moderate or greater PVL at 1-year follow-up. Mild PVL and new PPI remained frequent. Observed comparative signals should be interpreted as indirect hypothesis-generating findings.

title: Giant hiatal hernia as a contributing physiological stressor to cardiopulmonary dysfunction: a case report.
authors: Michelle Carrasquel-Alvarez; Mariana Valdez-Thomas; Maria Del Pilar Acosta
abstract:
Extracardiac thoracic pathology can significantly alter cardiac physiology and mimic primary heart disease, particularly in older adults with multiple comorbidities.
An 89-year-old woman with known aortic stenosis and heart failure presented with 1 week of progressive, positional dyspnoea and wheezing. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated severe global left ventricular systolic dysfunction with an estimated ejection fraction of approximately 30%, a dilated left atrium (dimension 4.77 cm, volume 100 mL), and markedly elevated filling pressures evidenced by a medial e' velocity of 3.16 cm/s, mitral E velocity of 103 cm/s, and E/e' ratio of 32.6. Aortic valve assessment revealed haemodynamic features of low-flow, low-gradient severe aortic stenosis, with a mean gradient of 26-28 mmHg, a valve area of 0.68 cm by continuity equation, a dimensionless index of 0.25, and a stroke volume index of 29.4 mL/m2. Notably, right ventricular size and systolic function were preserved despite estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 40-45 mmHg, a pattern physiologically discordant with the degree of left-sided dysfunction. Chest computed tomography revealed a giant paraesophageal hiatal hernia measuring 10-12 cm, with intrathoracic migration of the stomach causing extrinsic compression of the left atrium and posterior cardiac structures. Troponin was negative, and no electrocardiographic evidence of acute ischaemia was identified. The observed left ventricular dysfunction is likely multifactorial, with extracardiac compression acting as a contributing physiological stressor in the context of underlying low-flow severe aortic stenosis.
This case highlights the importance of recognizing extracardiac causes of cardiopulmonary deterioration and integrating multimodality imaging into diagnostic reasoning, particularly when haemodynamic findings are physiologically discordant.

title: Quantitative membranous septum area assessment with advanced three-dimensional CT visualization with a mixed reality-capable device.
authors: Cian O'Sullivan; Tsung-Ying Tsai; Hao-Wei Lee; Fei-Ran Chiou; Rachel Beatty; Maciej Stanuch; Andrzej Skalski; Akihiro Tobe; Garry P Duffy; Brendan Wilkins; Ryo Torii; Nicolo Piazza; Yoshinobu Onuma; Patrick W Serruys
abstract:
Permanent pacemaker implantation (PPI) rates remained elevated for patients receiving transcatheter aortic valve implantation for aortic stenosis (AS) and aortic regurgitation. Therefore, detailed assessment of the membranous septum (MS) anatomy is essential to understand the mechanism and mitigate risk. This study aims to examine the accuracy and reproducibility of a novel 3D hologram system to measure transcatheter aortic valve implantation-related aortic valvar complex anatomy and present a novel methodology to measure MS area with it.
Cardiac computer tomography series of AS, aortic regurgitation, and coronary artery disease (CAD) patient cohorts were analysed using CarnaLife Holo (MedApp SA, Kraków, Poland) to quantify and compare their MS areas. 3mensio Structural Heart was used as a benchmark comparator, with annulus area (AA) selected as the quantitative parameter. Intraclass correlation coefficient values between the software all exceeded 0.99, with no statistically significant difference noted between AA measurements. Bland-Altman plotting illustrated narrow boundaries of agreement, with no significant outliers. In interobserver agreement analysis for 3D hologram, AA measurements were not significantly different between two investigators (P = 0.906). No significant difference was found between the MS areas between the three cohorts after ANOVA testing (P = 0.1640).
3D holographic software provides a feasible and reproducible tool for visualising and measuring the aortic valvar complex anatomy. In addition, its ability to assess the shape, pattern, and area of the MS offers anatomic insights not readily available with other software.

title: Navigating Severe Aortic Stenosis in Hip Fracture Surgery: Perioperative Management and Surgical Timing.
authors: Richard Bui; Jen Li Dong; Austin Tran; Laasya Achanta; Jamal Hasoon; Alaa Abd-Elsayed; Alan D Kaye; Anvinh Nguyen
abstract: Severe aortic stenosis presents a significant challenge in patients requiring urgent hip fracture surgery. Although aortic stenosis increases the risk of cardiovascular complications and mortality, delaying fixation may independently contribute to morbidity, functional decline, and mortality. This creates a dilemma regarding whether to proceed directly to surgery or delay fracture repair for aortic valve intervention. This review examines management of patients with severe aortic stenosis pending urgent hip fracture surgery, with emphasis on timing, preoperative evaluation, anesthetic selection, and hemodynamic management. Current evidence suggests that asymptomatic patients with preserved left ventricular systolic function and stable hemodynamics may often undergo timely fracture fixation with appropriate monitoring. In contrast, symptomatic patients, those with ventricular dysfunction or hemodynamic instability, and patients with particularly severe disease may require evaluation for valvular intervention. When intervention is indicated, transcatheter aortic valve replacement may offer a more rapid treatment in certain patients, while balloon aortic valvuloplasty may serve as a temporizing strategy. For patients proceeding directly to fracture fixation, preservation of preload, systemic vascular resistance, coronary perfusion, and sinus rhythm is essential. Current evidence does not establish a clear superiority of general versus neuraxial anesthesia, supporting individualized anesthetic planning and avoidance of abrupt hemodynamic changes. Ultimately, management should balance the risks of delaying fracture fixation against the risks of surgery through coordinated, multidisciplinary decision-making.

title: Tailored Calibration Approach for Hemodynamic Boundary Conditions in CT-FFR
authors: Yoon A Kim; Daebeom Park; Doyeon Hwang; Seokhun Yang; Sang‐Hyeon Park; Chang‐Wook Nam; Joon‐Hyung Doh; Hyun Kuk Kim; Yongcheol Kim; Eun Ju Chun; Bon‐Kwon Koo
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Computed tomography-derived fractional flow reserve (CT-FFR) uses standardized boundary conditions that cannot represent individual patient characteristics. We developed a calibration method to individualize boundary conditions using invasive fractional flow reserve (FFR) measurement. This study assessed the feasibility and impact on prediction of lesion-specific pressure drops (ΔFFR), post-percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) FFR, and high-risk plaque (HRP) discrimination. METHODS: This retrospective multicenter study analyzed 79 patients with single left anterior descending lesions. Lumped parameter models were used to calibrate optimal boundary conditions by iteratively minimizing differences between invasive FFR and CT-FFR. HRP was assessed using an artificial intelligence-enabled analysis system, defined as low attenuation plaque, positive remodeling, or both. Discrimination performance was evaluated using ΔCT-FFR and CT-FFR gradient. RESULTS: In 79 patients (median age 65.5 years, 77.2% male), median angiographic percent diameter stenosis 60.0%, median invasive FFR was 0.83 and CT-FFR was 0.81 before calibration. Following calibration, FFR correlation improved from 0.590 to 0.997 (p<0.001). ΔFFR correlation increased from 0.490 to 0.823 (p<0.001). Post-PCI validation showed correlation improvement from 0.440 to 0.871 (p=0.002). HRP discrimination improved for ΔCT-FFR (area under the curve [AUC], 0.62 to 0.70; p=0.018) and CT-FFR gradient (AUC, 0.62 to 0.69; p=0.032). CONCLUSIONS: Individualized boundary condition calibration using invasive FFR enables accurate prediction of lesion-specific hemodynamics and post-intervention physiology, showing potential for enhanced procedural planning and risk stratification in patients undergoing coronary angiography.

title: Overlapping Diabetes- and CKD-Driven Vascular Phenotypes of Peripheral Artery Disease: A Limb-First Framework for Chronic Limb-Threatening Ischemia
authors: Ju-Yeon Lee; Ji‐Yong Jang; Chang‐Myung Oh
abstract: Peripheral artery disease (PAD) and chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI) impose an increasing global burden. Although procedural success exceeds 90%, 1-year amputation rates remain >20%, highlighting a disconnect between technical success and clinical benefit. PAD is commonly treated as a uniform atherosclerotic condition; however, distinct biological phenotypes drive heterogeneous outcomes and require individualized management. Diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease (CKD), present in >70% of patients with CLTI, promote divergent pathological mechanisms. Diabetes is characterized by intimal inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, and microangiopathy, whereas CKD is dominated by medial calcification due to disordered mineral metabolism, limiting the reliability of the ankle-brachial index. Diabetes-CKD coexistence, observed in 35-50% of cases, produces combined occlusive and rigid vascular features and carries a disproportionately high risk of poor wound healing, major amputation, and early mortality-a burden that current lesion-centric approaches consistently fail to adequately address. This review integrates mechanistic insights, diagnostic considerations, and clinical evidence supporting phenotype-based management. We propose a practical framework that aligns phenotype recognition with targeted strategies: endovascular intervention with metabolic optimization for diabetes-predominant PAD, calcium-modifying approaches or bypass surgery for CKD-predominant PAD, and early prognostic counseling with palliative integration for combined phenotypes. This limb-first paradigm reframes revascularization as a biologically informed intervention and provides evidence-based pathways to improve outcomes in contemporary CLTI care.

title: Three-Year Outcomes of Drug-Eluting Stents, Drug-Coated Balloons, and Non-Drug-Eluting Devices in Native Femoropopliteal Artery Disease: An Analysis of the K-VIS ELLA Registry
authors: Jaeoh Lee; In Tae Jin; Chul‐Min Ahn; Jae‐Hwan Lee; Pil‐Ki Min; Ji‐Yong Jang; Chang‐Hwan Yoon; Seung‐Whan Lee; Young Jin Youn; Cheol Woong Yu; Byung‐Hee Hwang; Ae‐Young Her; Jung‐Kyu Han; Sang-Min Kim; Woong Chol Kang; Wonmook Hwang; Eui Im; Yong Seong Seo; Ju Han Kim; Tae‐Hoon Kim; Han‐Young Jin; Woo‐Young Chung; Byung Sik Kim; Chang-Bae Sohn; Seung‐Hyuk Choi; Donghoon Choi; Young‐Guk Ko; On behalf of the K-VIS ELLA investigators
abstract: Background: Although drug-eluting devices have demonstrated improved efficacy in femoropopliteal artery (FPA) disease, evidence on their long-term clinical outcomes in realworld practice remains limited.Methods: Using data from the multicenter Korean Vascular Intervention Society Endovascular Therapy in Lower Limb Artery Disease registry, 4,193 symptomatic native FPA limbs were analyzed.Treatments included non-drug-eluting devices, comprising plain old balloon angioplasty (n = 1,194) and bare-metal stents (n = 1,510), and drug-eluting devices, comprising drug-eluting stents (DES; n = 347) and drug-coated balloons (DCB; n = 1,142).The primary endpoint was clinically driven target lesion revascularization (CD-TLR) at 3 years.Inverse probability of treatment weighting was used to balance baseline characteristics.Results: After weighting, baseline characteristics were well balanced across groups.The mean patient age was 69.7 years, the mean lesion length was approximately 170.4 mm, and 59% of lesions were classified as Trans-Atlantic Inter-Society Consensus II C/D.At 3 years, DES and DCB were associated with significantly lower cumulative incidences of CD-TLR than non-drug-eluting devices (DES, 22.4% vs. 26.5%;adjusted hazard ratio [HR], 0.62; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.42-0.91;P = 0.014; DCB, 20.5% vs. 26.5%;adjusted HR, 0.54; 95% CI, 0.40-0.73;P < 0.001).The CD-TLR rate did not differ significantly between DES and DCB.Rates of major amputation and all-cause mortality were similar across groups.Conclusions: In patients with symptomatic native FPA disease, endovascular treatment with DES or DCB was associated with a lower 3-year risk of CD-TLR than treatment with nondrug-eluting devices, without an increased risk of mortality.

title: Left Atrial Functional Parameters and Left Ventricular Reverse Remodeling After Aortic Valve Replacement in Severe Aortic Stenosis
authors: Na Chen; Yongxin Li; Siqi Cao; Wenhui Gu; Huiyu Tang; Siyao Sun; Tao Cong; Haibo Wu; Jun Wu
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Left ventricular reverse remodeling (LVRR) after aortic valve replacement (AVR) varies in severe aortic stenosis (AS). We evaluated whether preoperative left atrial (LA)-derived functional indices were associated with structural LVRR (S-LVRR) and functional LVRR (F-LVRR). METHODS: This retrospective 2-center study included 139 adults with severe AS undergoing surgical or transcatheter AVR and follow-up echocardiography after a median of 6.1 months. S-LVRR was defined as normalization of left ventricular (LV) mass index, and F-LVRR as sex-specific recovery of absolute LV global longitudinal strain. Separate adjusted logistic models assessed LA reservoir strain (LASr), LA stiffness index (LASI), LA reservoir work, and LA volumetric/mechanical coupling index, with supportive sensitivity analyses. RESULTS: S-LVRR and F-LVRR occurred in 58 (41.7%) and 42 (30.2%) patients, respectively. Higher LASr and lower LASI were independently associated with S-LVRR (odds ratio [OR] per 1-standard deviation increase, 2.48; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.37-4.49 and OR, 0.32; 95% CI, 0.13-0.79) and F-LVRR (OR, 7.41; 95% CI, 2.70-20.32 and OR, 0.01; 95% CI, 0.00-0.15). LASr remained robust across sensitivity analyses, whereas LASI was attenuated in change-based analyses. CONCLUSIONS: In severe AS, preserved preoperative LASr and lower LASI were associated with postoperative LVRR after AVR. LASr was the most consistent LA-derived marker and may complement conventional LV assessment pending prospective validation.

title: Fluid-structure Interaction Analysis of Intracranial Atherosclerosis Disease (ICAD): Moderate and Severe Stenosis Cases
authors: M. N. I. Muhamad Nazri; Adi Azriff Basri; M. Tamagawa; K. Sagara; A. H. K. Yusof Khan; E. R. M. Tohit; M. F. Al-Khafiz Kamis; M. T. H. Sultan
abstract: This study investigated the effects of Intracranial Atherosclerosis Disease (ICAD) severity on vessel hemodynamics and structural response using one-way Fluid–Structure Interaction (FSI) simulations performed in ANSYS 25, comparing moderate (50% stenosis) and severe (70% stenosis) cases. A validation experiment was also conducted to support the simulation results. Key parameters including velocity profile, pressure drop, wall shear stress, flow vectors, total deformation, equivalent stress, and equivalent elastic strain were analyzed throughout the cardiac cycle. The results showed that increasing ICAD severity significantly altered both hemodynamic and structural behavior. Compared to 50% stenosis, the 70% stenosis model exhibited a 70.5% increase in maximum velocity, 6.74% higher pressure, and 20.9% higher wall shear stress. During peak systole, pressure drops were 6.6% for 70% stenosis and 1.1% for 50% stenosis. Structural responses also increased, with deformation, equivalent stress, and elastic strain rising by approximately 18%, 17%, and 18.1%, respectively, concentrated near the stenotic region.

title: Neuroselective Sensory-Over-Motor Dissociation, Rapid Blockade Onset, and Hemodynamic Autoregulation With 10 μg Intrathecal Dexmedetomidine in High-Risk Orthopedic and Gynecological Surgery: An Observational Analytic Case Series
authors: Muhammad Adiwibowo; Muhamad Farlyzhar Yusuf
journal: Open Access Indonesian Journal of Medical Reviews
abstract: Background: Subarachnoid block gives dense blockade for orthopedic and gynecological surgery, but plain local anesthetics give brief analgesia. Intrathecal dexmedetomidine (DXM), a selective α₂-adrenergic agonist, prolongs block in low-risk patients. Data in high-risk patients are scarce. Objective: To describe block onset, regression, pain scores, and hemodynamic course after 10 μg of intrathecal DXM added to hyperbaric bupivacaine in four high-risk patients. Methods: Four consecutive women (29–73 years) were operated on at Dr. Saiful Anwar Regional General Hospital, Malang, Indonesia (Protocol: CMHC/EC/IRB/2026/0814). Each received 0.5% hyperbaric bupivacaine (15–20 mg) plus 10 μg DXM, by L4–L5 subarachnoid block (Cases 1–3) or combined spinal-epidural anesthesia (Case 4). Onset, hemodynamics, and Numerical Rating Scale (NRS) pain scores were recorded from T₀ to T₄. Results: All patients reached the target block (T6–T10). Sensory onset was ≤ 1 min and Modified Bromage 2 motor block appeared at 3 min; the published mean to Bromage 3 with 5 μg is 11.6 min. Motor inhibition lasted 300 min and analgesia 300–360 min (mean 330 ± 24.5 min), with NRS 0–2 in the first 4 h and 3–4 at 5–6 h. MAP was 70 mmHg in a post-stroke patient. A fall to 50/30 mmHg during bone curettage resolved with 1,000 mL crystalloid and ephedrine. Multimodal and neuraxial analgesia were also given. Conclusion: In four patients, 10 μg of intrathecal DXM was followed by rapid block onset and 5–6 h of analgesia, with no recorded respiratory depression. The series cannot establish effect or mechanism, so controlled studies are needed.

title: Phenylephrine-provoked endoscopy reveals an occult Dieulafoy’s lesion in a duodenal diverticulum: A case report and review of literature
authors: Yu-Jie Shen; Jiao-Jiao Song; Xiao-Qin Liu; Feng-Ling Hu
abstract: BACKGROUND The diagnosis of a Dieulafoy’s lesion located within a duodenal diverticulum (DD) presents a significant challenge, particularly during nonbleeding intervals. Pharmacological provocation has been proposed for obscure gastrointestinal bleeding. However, experience with provocative endoscopy is largely confined to antithrombotic-based protocols, which are associated with a delayed and unpredictable bleeding onset. The use of vasopressors as pharmacological provocation agents for endoscopic localization has not been previously explored. CASE SUMMARY We report the case of a 53-year-old woman with recurrent obscure gastrointestinal bleeding and a haemoglobin level ranging from 50 g/L to 84 g/L. Enhanced abdominal computed tomography showed multiple duodenal diverticula (DDs) in the distal duodenum, with a prominent arterial vessel traversing the wall of one diverticulum. Multiple standard endoscopies revealed fresh clots in the DDs but no definitive bleeding source during nonbleeding intervals. With clinical suspicion of a vascular lesion in the DDs, we administered phenylephrine to induce controlled hypertension for provocative endoscopy, which led to active bleeding from the previously concealed lesion within minutes. Using a colonoscope to enhance distal duodenal visualization, we successfully achieved endoscopic localization and haemostasis in the distal duodenum. The provocation was effective, with no recurrent bleeding or adverse events during a 2-month follow-up. CONCLUSION Phenylephrine-provoked endoscopy assists in localizing quiescent occult Dieulafoy’s lesion in a distal duodenal diverticulum with a colonoscope.

title: Lipoprotein(a) in clinical practice: From genetic risk assessment to therapeutic silencing
authors: Lucas Dias Feliciano; João P C Freire; Caio Ferraz Lopes; Pedro H M Lima; Juan M C Costa; Fabrício Freire de Melo
abstract: Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is a genetically determined lipoprotein particle increasingly recognized as an independent and causal risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and calcific aortic valve disease. Its unique structure, composed of a low-density lipoprotein-like particle bound to apolipoprotein(a), confers both atherogenic and proinflammatory properties that distinguish it from other circulating lipoproteins. This review examines the molecular structure of Lp(a), its genetic determinants, and the mechanisms linking elevated Lp(a) levels to atherogenesis and vascular inflammation. We critically discuss the role of apolipoprotein(a) isoform variability, kringle domain polymorphisms, oxidized phospholipid transport, endothelial dysfunction, inflammatory signaling pathways, and thrombogenic pathways in mediating cardiovascular risk. In addition, we review current approaches for laboratory assessment and summarize emerging therapeutic strategies aimed at selectively lowering Lp(a), including antisense oligonucleotides and small interfering RNA-based therapies. Recent advances in molecular therapeutics have demonstrated substantial reductions in circulating Lp(a) concentrations, although definitive evidence regarding cardiovascular outcome benefits is still under investigation. A better understanding of Lp(a) biology and its inflammatory and atherogenic mechanisms may improve risk stratification and support the development of personalized preventive and therapeutic strategies in cardiovascular medicine.

title: Mechanisms, clinical translation, and future perspectives of liver-mediated immunoprotection in combined organ transplantation
authors: Zhengwei Zhao; Yu-Guo Chen; Guang-Yi Wang
abstract: Owing to its unique tolerogenic immune microenvironment, the liver can confer substantial immunologic protection on concurrently transplanted allogeneic grafts in combined organ transplantation. This review summarizes the molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying liver-mediated immunoprotection, including antigen presentation by liver sinusoidal endothelial cells and tolerogenic dendritic cells, enrichment of regulatory T cells, clonal deletion of donor-reactive T cells, clearance of donor-specific antibodies, and the establishment of microchimerism. We further synthesize clinical outcome data from combined liver-intestinal transplantation and multivisceral transplantation, and evaluate the translational potential of optimized immunosuppressive strategies, cell-based therapies, and emerging technologies such as normothermic machine perfusion. Although current evidence supports the immunoprotective role of the liver, its precise molecular mechanisms remain incompletely defined and require further validation. Prospective multicenter studies are also warranted.

title: Pacing in adults with complex congenital heart disease: A narrative minireview
authors: Vasileios Papaioannou; Julia Jones; Fahmi Faraz; David Mayhew; Archana Rao; Matthew Kahn; Sarah Moharem Elgamal; Reza Ashrafi
abstract: Congenital heart disease (CHD) is a growing health care problem, as more pediatric patients survive to adulthood every year as the number of patients with complex conditions also increases. As more patients survive, there has been an increase in the need for pacemaker procedures. Historically, there has been a focus on epicardial pacing in the most complex groups. In this review, we examine the background epidemiology, existing evidence for pacing, extraction data in three of the most complex CHD groups- transposition of the great arteries with an atrial switch procedure, patients palliated with a Fontan procedure and univentricular hearts. In this expert narrative review, we have used a broad search strategy of PubMed supplemented with evidence where available from non-congenital cohorts. The evidence in these most complex cohorts can be limited to expert centre opinion, small numbers and mixed paediatric/adult data. We discuss below the available data, the limitations and the novel approaches available in centres to deal with the most complex conditions such as conduction system pacing and leadless pacing with promising results albeit in expert centres only. Whilst current applicability to a wider range of institutions is not yet suggested by the paper, this review hopefully illustrates potential options for consideration and research in the future.

title: Practical Solutions to Common TAVI Complications
authors: Herbert Kroon
abstract: Aortic valve stenosis Calcific aortic valve degeneration mainly affects the elderly population. Approximately 15% of elderly patients have some degree of aortic stenosis (AS)1. Untreated severe AS will lead to heart failure, angina and/or syncope and approximately half of patients will expire within 2 years after symptom onset1, 2. Historically, open heart surgery was the only treatment for severe AS. However, advanced age was a dominant argument to defer surgery. Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) was contrived as a less invasive alternative to surgery and to fulfill this unmet clinical need. After the first-in-human procedure in 2002, TAVI matured into a guideline recommended treatment of symptomatic severe AS in elderly patients across the entire risk spectrum3-7. Peri-procedural embolization Operator experience, improved planning and implantation strategies and multiple device iterations including smaller profile, repositioning ability and outer sealing fabric converted TAVI into a reproducible and relatively safe procedure8. However, the “Big Five” of complications in the modern TAVI era remain 1) access site complications and bleedings, 2) paravalvular leakage (PVL), 3) acute kidney injury (AKI), 4) conduction disturbances including the need for permanent pacemaker implantation (PPI) and 5) stroke9. Up to 5% of patients suffer a neurological event after TAVI, mainly within the first 48 hours8, 10, 11. This finding suggests a direct causative role with the transcatheter valve implantation itself. Transcranial Doppler and brain Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) studies revealed debris embolization towards the brain and new brain lesions after TAVI in the vast majority of patients12-15. Most of these embolizations remain clinically silent at first sight but may be linked to neurocognitive decline and frank dementia16. Embolic protection devices (EPD) have been developed to deflect or capture embolized debris on its way to the brain and may possibly reduce brain lesions and neurological events including stroke and neurocognitive decline. Part I of this thesis adds perspective to the etiopathology of TAVI related stroke and the mechanism of action of the current spectrum of cerebral embolic protection devices. We also present insights into the microscopic analysis of debris that was captured with filters during TAVI procedures. Vascular access and complications 1 TAVI typically requires large bore femoral artery access. By default, larger arteriotomies are at higher risk for access site complications and bleedings. A completely percutaneous approach relies on vascular access closure devices (VCD) to manage the arteriotomy and provide patent hemostasis. TAVI in low to intermediate risk patients is associated with a major vascular complication rate ranging between 2 and 8%4, 11. The conventional closure technique is based on sutures and most access site complications after TAVI procedures are related to closure device failure17. A collagen plug based closure device was introduced as an alternative to sutures. Part II of this thesis addresses vascular complications and provides information on clinical outcomes with collagen plug-based VCD. TAVI-related conduction disturbances Acquired conduction disturbances after TAVI are frequent and may lead to heart failure (re-) admissions and impaired long-term prognosis18-22. The atrioventricular bundle pierces the membranous septum between the right and non-coronary cusp of the aortic valve and surfaces along the left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT), which makes it vulnerable to contact pressure by the implanted transcatheter heart valve (THV) during TAVI23, 24. New left bundle branch block (LBBB) and third-degree atrioventricular block (AV3B) requiring PPI occur in up to a third and quarter of patients, respectively18-22. These conduction disturbances may be transient or remain permanent which is clinically relevant in view of in-hospital stay and overall healthcare costs. Unfortunately, there are no uniform definitions to describe conduction dynamics post-TAVI. Inconsistent reporting makes the interpretation of the literature on this topic challenging. Part III of this thesis will elaborate on what is currently known about the incidence of newly acquired conduction disturbances after TAVI and studies specific features on the baseline and postprocedural electrocardiogram (ECG) to predict conduction dynamics. These insights may help determine the need and timing of PPI and adjust hospital discharge policies.

title: Optimal experimental design with k-space data: application to inverse hemodynamics
authors: Miriam Löcke; Ahmed Attia; Dariusz Uciński; Cristóbal Bertoglio
abstract: Subject-specific cardiovascular models rely on parameter estimation using measurements such as 4D Flow magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data. However, acquiring high-resolution, high-fidelity functional flow data is costly and burdensome for patients. As a result, there is growing interest in using highly undersampled MRI data to reduce acquisition time and cost while maximizing the information gained from the data. Recent examples include inverse problems that estimate boundary conditions of aortic blood flow from highly undersampled k-space data. The undersampled data are selected based on a predefined sampling mask, which can significantly influence the performance and quality of the inverse problem solution. While many established sampling patterns exist for collecting undersampled data, it remains unclear how to select the best sampling pattern for a given set of inference parameters. In this paper, we propose an optimal experimental design (OED) framework for MRI measurements in k-space, aiming to find optimal masks for estimating specific parameters of the fluid flow models directly from k-space. We demonstrate that masks optimized using OED consistently outperform conventional sampling patterns in terms of parameter estimation accuracy and variance, enabling a 10x reduction in acquisition time while maintaining accuracy.

title: Trio-based whole-exome sequencing and minigene assay identify a novel MYH11 splice site variant (c.2997 + 5G > C) in recurrent fetal megacystis
authors: Wenwen Li; Yeqing Qian; Pan Gao; Lihong Fan; Xinli Zhang; Xuekui Pan; Guosong Shen; Qiongshan Li; Xueping Shen
abstract: Background Megacystis-microcolon-intestinal hypoperistalsis syndrome (MMIHS) is a severe visceral myopathy attributed to defects in smooth muscle contraction. Although pathogenic variants in genes such as ACTG2 , LMOD1 , MYLK , MYH9 , and MYH11 have been associated with MMIHS, the complete genotypic spectrum remains inadequately characterized. Methods We reported a non-consanguineous Chinese family exhibiting recurrent fetal megacystis. Trio-based whole-exome sequencing (Trio-WES) was performed on the parents and the affected fetus. The functional impact of a novel splice site variant identified in the MYH11 gene was assessed using a Minigene splicing assay in vitro . Results Trio-based whole-exome sequencing identified compound heterozygous variants in the MYH11 gene: a maternally inherited 1.9 Mb deletion encompassing MYH11 at 16q13.11, and a novel paternally inherited splice site variant (c.2997 + 5G > C). Initially classified as a variant of uncertain significance (VUS), the pathogenicity of the c.2997 + 5G > C variant was confirmed through functional validation, which demonstrated aberrant splicing. This confirmation facilitated a definitive prenatal diagnosis. Conclusions This study identifies a novel pathogenic splice site variant in MYH11 associated with MMIHS and provides functional evidence supporting its role in the disease’s etiology. Our findings highlight the critical importance of integrating genomic analyses with functional assays to refine interpretation of VUS, expand the mutational spectrum of MMIHS, and improve genetic counseling for affected families.

title: Right Anterior Thoracotomy Aortic Valve Replacement: Technique and Early Outcomes in 156 Patients
authors: Daniel Shell; Andrew Mekhail; Ploy Jaithong; Cheng‐Hon Yap
abstract: Background: Right anterior thoracotomy aortic valve replacement (RAT-AVR) is an established minimally invasive alternative to conventional sternotomy, but published experience largely reflects late-experience series from specialised centres. Data describing operative technique and early outcomes during real-world adoption remain limited. Methods: We describe our operative technique and early outcomes in 156 consecutive intended isolated RAT-AVR procedures performed by a single surgeon between January 2015 and November 2025. Operative times were compared between the first 50 and subsequent 106 cases and assessed using cumulative sum analysis. Results: Median age was 70 years and median EuroSCORE II was 1.00% [IQR 0.71–1.56]. Peripheral cannulation was used in most cases, with central cannulation employed selectively. Mechanical and biological prostheses spanning 19–29 mm were implanted, demonstrating that prosthesis choice was not restricted in this cohort. Median cardiopulmonary bypass and cross-clamp times were 109 and 79 min, respectively. Both were shorter after the first 50 cases (120.5 versus 106.0 min, p = 0.003; 85.5 versus 77.0 min, p = 0.048). Conversion to sternotomy occurred in two patients, both of whom survived to discharge and 30 days. Thirty-day mortality was 2/156 (1.3%). Conclusions: This consecutive single-surgeon experience supports the feasibility and early safety of RAT-AVR in selected patients, with operative efficiency improving during adoption. RAT-AVR represents a pragmatic minimally invasive option for isolated surgical aortic valve replacement.

title: Antihypertensive treatment – achievements and perspectives in Europe by 2026 Italian, Swiss and Norwegian patient care
authors: Sverre Erik Kjeldsen; Jørgen A. Gravning; Mathis K. Stokke; Michel Burnier; Guido M. Grassi; Giuseppe Mancia
abstract: PURPOSE: The aim of this perspective review paper is to provide a concise overview of selected aspects of contemporary hypertension care in Norway, Switzerland, and Italy; European countries with populations of approximately 5.5, 9, and 61 million inhabitants, respectively. These countries show remarkably similar prevalences of hypertension, as well as comparable proportions of hypertensive patients who are diagnosed, treated, and controlled. METHODS: Each country has contributed to the development of hypertension management in distinctive ways. This is illustrated by the evolution of hypertension care in the three countries-which advanced hypertension management through different but complementary contributions. RESULTS: Italy has provided extensive clinical and research expertise, together with sustained engagement in the European Society of Hypertension and in the development of European guidelines. Norway has been strongly involved in the design and conduct of many large clinical trials that helped define the clinical evidence base in the field, and with general practitioners as investigators. Also, the government financed major surveys and epidemiological studies with blood pressure (BP) as a key variable including collecting data for modern risk assessment in old people (SCORE2-Old People). Switzerland, for its part, made important contributions to the development of new antihypertensive drugs, particularly blockers of the renin-angiotensin system and calcium antagonists. Switzerland was also among the first European countries to accept, promote, and reimburse ambulatory blood pressure monitoring performed by general practitioners, already by the late 1980s. CONCLUSION: We summarise novelties in text boxes besides basic principles, recent clarifications, and important unresolved issues, supported by selected key references.

title: Transcatheter aortic valve replacement in very severe aortic stenosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Yuval Avidan; Hussein Sliman; Amir Yahav; Hisham Atwan; Sewar Nassar; Moataz Tarabih; Hadi Fowaz; Salim Adawi; Amir Aker
abstract: Patients with very severe aortic stenosis (VSAS) are regarded to carry a poorer prognosis than patients with severe aortic stenosis (SAS). While current guidelines endorse earlier aortic valve replacement, evidence supporting the safety and efficacy of transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) in this subgroup remains limited. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to clarify clinical outcomes following TAVR in VSAS patients. From inception to March 2025, we systematically searched Medline, Embase, Scopus and Cochrane databases, for studies comparing TAVR outcomes in SAS and VSAS. Primary endpoints included 1-year all-cause mortality and heart failure hospitalizations. Secondary endpoints included procedural complications, and 30-day outcomes. Five observational studies including 2,430 patients (1,724 with SAS and 706 with VSAS) were analyzed. The mean age was 82.4 years, with 64.5% female. VSAS was associated with lower 1-year all-cause mortality (OR = 0.73; 95% CI: 0.57–0.94) and heart failure readmissions (OR = 0.57; 95% CI: 0.36–0.92). Stroke risk trended higher in VSAS (OR = 1.72; 95% CI: 0.87–3.40), while pacemaker implantation rates, degree of paravalvular leak, and 30-day mortality were comparable. Patients with VSAS demonstrate greater benefit in terms of 1-year all-cause mortality and heart failure readmissions after TAVR compared to those with SAS, without an associated increase in procedural complications. Prospective studies with extended follow-up are required to validate these observations.

title: Analysis code: Circulating interleukin-6 concentration mis-specifies the exposure in aortic stenosis (receptor-level Mendelian randomization)
authors: Jiacheng Rong; Yuquan Xie; Shuang; Huang; Liao; Pu
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Complete executable analysis code (54 Python + 10 R scripts, shared utilities, and unit tests) for a two-sample, dual-platform, three-outcome bidirectional Mendelian randomization study applying a pre-specified four-tier evidence standard to 111 circulating inflammatory proteins against calcific aortic valve stenosis. Identifies attenuated interleukin-6 receptor signaling (rs2228145) as the sole Tier-4, lipoprotein(a)-independent drug target, and includes an exposure-definition contrast showing the inferred direction reverses with the exposure label at the IL6R shedding locus, a per-exposure power audit of non-replicated prior cytokine claims, and a 2,470-endpoint PheWAS safety profile. All inputs are public or approved-access GWAS summary statistics; no individual-level data are included.

title: The Stratified Association of Left Atrial Volume Index and Dynamic Change of Pulmonary Arterial Pressure on Prognosis After Catheter Ablation in Patients With Persistent Atrial Fibrillation
authors: Yoon Jung Park; Jiwon Park; Min-Su Jung; Tae-Wan Chung; Hee Jeong Lee; Jongmin Hwang; Hyungseop Kim; Hyoung‐Seob Park; In‐Cheol Kim
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Catheter ablation is a key strategy for rhythm control in atrial fibrillation (AF), yet recurrence remains frequent, particularly in persistent AF. This study evaluated echocardiographic parameters to predict post-ablation recurrence. METHODS: Patients with persistent AF who underwent catheter ablation and had both pre- and post-echocardiography between 2011 and March 2022 were enrolled. Post-ablation echocardiography was conducted within one week. Patients were stratified by median left atrial volume index (LAVI, 62 mL/m²) and pulmonary artery systolic pressure (PASP, 24 mmHg) on transthoracic echocardiography. The association between pre- and post-ablation PASP, stratified by LAVI size, and AF recurrence was then evaluated. RESULTS: -VASc scores. Kaplan-Meier analysis demonstrated the lowest AF recurrence rates in this group (p<0.01). Among patients with LAVI ≤62 mL/m², those with elevated pre- and post-ablation PASP had the highest recurrence rate (51%), while those with low pre- and post-ablation PASP had the lowest recurrence rate (19%) at one year. In patients with LAVI >62 mL/m², recurrence rates were generally higher (average 42%), and were less influenced by PASP variation. However, there was a trend toward a lower recurrence rate (32%) in patients with elevated pre-ablation PASP and low post-ablation PASP. CONCLUSIONS: Integrating LAVI with changes in PASP showed differences in post-ablation recurrence rate in patients with persistent AF. Pre- and post-ablation echocardiographic assessment of PASP can provide important insights for post-procedural management.

title: Intracranial Subdural Empyema Associated with Streptococcus Dysgalactiae Subsp. Equisimilis in a Patient with Chronic Subdural Hematomas
authors: Ryo Yonai; Ryota Sato; Takashi Shinzato
abstract: A 73-year-old man with conservatively managed bilateral chronic subdural hematomas presented with fever and vomiting, followed by a seizure and impaired consciousness. Craniotomy revealed subdural pus, supporting intracranial subdural empyema arising in these hematomas. Streptococcus dysgalactiae subsp. equisimilis (SDSE) was recovered from blood and subdural cultures, although a polymicrobial infection could not be excluded because subdural sampling followed antibiotic initiation. He improved after drainage and four weeks of antibiotic treatment. SDSE bacteremia with neurological deterioration should prompt consideration of subdural empyema. Hematogenous seeding was considered to be the most likely route of infection.

title: Combined Mitral and Tricuspid Transcatheter Edge-to-Edge Repair: Evidence, Patient Selection, and Procedural Strategy
authors: Georgios  E Papadopoulos; Vlasis N. Ninios; Ilias Ninios; Sotirios Evangelou; Apostolia Marvaki; Maria Kalaitzoglou; Andreas Ioannides; Andrew V. Xanthopoulos; John S. Skoularigis; Grigorios Giamouzis
abstract: Concomitant mitral regurgitation (MR) and tricuspid regurgitation (TR) constitute an interconnected multivalvular syndrome, but correction of MR does not consistently reverse TR. This narrative review examines TR evolution after mitral transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (M-TEER), patient selection, imaging, procedural strategies, and evidence for treatment of both valves. Combined TEER denotes bivalvular treatment, performed during the same session or in stages. Observational cohorts report TR improvement in approximately one-third of broadly selected patients after M-TEER, with substantial variation according to baseline severity, response definition, and follow-up. Persistent or new-onset TR is associated with adverse outcomes; these associations do not establish that subsequent tricuspid intervention improves survival. Comparative registries suggest potential clinical benefit from combined treatment, whereas uncontrolled series primarily establish technical feasibility in selected patients at experienced centers. Treatment timing remains uncertain because randomized comparisons of isolated, same-session, and staged strategies are unavailable. The proposed Heart Team framework integrates lesion-specific indications, anatomical suitability, anticipated TR reversibility, physiological reserve, and patient goals. It is an unvalidated discussion aid rather than a treatment recommendation. Randomized strategy trials are needed to establish incremental clinical benefit, comparative safety, and optimal timing.

title: Waterston's groove vs right atrial transseptal approach for resection of left atrial myxoma: A five-year retrospective cohort study at a single academic heart center in Indonesia
authors: Rafaela Andira Ledyastatin; Yan Efrata Sembiring
abstract: Objective: Cardiac myxoma is the most common primary cardiac tumor and most frequently arises in the left atrium (LA). Surgical excision is curative, but the LA can be approached either directly through the posterior interatrial groove (Waterston's groove) or indirectly through the right atrium (RA) and interatrial septum (transseptal approach); comparative data on these two approaches remain limited. The objective of the study was to retrospectively analyze cases of LA myxoma treated surgically at a single Indonesian academic heart center and compare baseline characteristics, tumor features, intraoperative variables, postoperative complications, and in-hospital outcomes between the Waterston's groove and RA transseptal approaches. Methods: This retrospective cohort study was conducted at the Department of Thoracic, Cardiac and Vascular Surgery, Dr. Soetomo General Academic Hospital, Surabaya, Indonesia. Patients who underwent surgical excision of a pathologically confirmed LA myxoma between January 2017 and December 2022 were identified from the departmental surgical registry. One patient with a RA (not LA) tumor was excluded, leaving 25 patients for analysis (Waterston's groove, n=14; right atrial transseptal, n=11). Data were compared using the Mann-Whitney U and Fisher's exact tests. Results: Patients were predominantly female (15/25, 60.0%), with a mean age of 48.5 (13.5) years. Groups did not differ by age, sex, and comorbidity distribution (all p>0.05). Tumors were large (>4 cm in maximum dimension) in 22/25 patients (88.0%); all 14 Waterston's-groove tumors exceeded 4 cm, compared with 8/11 (72.7%) in the transseptal group, a difference that did not reach statistical significance (p=0.072). Mean cardiopulmonary bypass time was 95.6 (44.9) minutes in the Waterston's-groove group versus 101.7 (33.3) minutes in the transseptal group (p=0.827), and mean aortic cross-clamp time was 66.3 (39.5) versus 61.4 (35.7) minutes, respectively (p=0.978); neither difference was statistically significant. A concomitant mitral or tricuspid valve procedures were performed in 11/25 patients (44.0%), without a significant difference between groups (p=0.689), however concomitant atrial septal defect closure was more often in transseptal approach group (p=0.023). Postoperative arrhythmia occurred in 3/25 patients (12.0%; 7.1% Waterston's groove vs. 18.2% transseptal, (p=0.565). There was no in-hospital mortality and no residual tumor in either group. Conclusion: In this single-center series, Waterston's groove and RA transseptal resection of LA myxoma achieved comparable, safe in-hospital outcomes, with no statistically significant difference in cardiopulmonary bypass time, aortic cross-clamp time, or perioperative complications. Waterston's groove was used exclusively for tumors larger than 4 cm, suggesting that tumor size may influence approach selection at our center; this observation should be tested in larger, prospective, multicenter studies with structured long-term follow-up.

title: SCORE Procedure for Repair of Rheumatic Heart Disease in a Patient With a History of PBMV
